people.name: George Washington
people.subtitle: 1st President · The founding farmer
people.biography: Surveyor, soldier, and farmer, Washington helped establish the presidency and returned to Mount Vernon after two terms.

image.attribution: Gilbert Stuart, George Washington, 1803. Clark Art Institute; reproduction via Wikimedia Commons.
image.rights: Public-domain painting and faithful reproduction; artist died in 1828.

people.name: Thomas Jefferson
people.subtitle: 3rd President · A mind in motion
people.biography: A writer and architect who championed liberty while enslaving people, Jefferson’s life exposes profound contradictions in the founding era.

image.attribution: Rembrandt Peale, Thomas Jefferson, 1800. Official presidential portrait reproduction via Wikimedia Commons.
image.rights: Public-domain painting; official U.S. Executive Office reproduction is public domain.

people.name: Abraham Lincoln
people.subtitle: 16th President · From cabin to capital
people.biography: Largely self-educated, Lincoln became a lawyer and led the Union during the Civil War.

image.attribution: Alexander Gardner, Abraham Lincoln, 1863. Mead Art Museum; reproduction via Wikimedia Commons.
image.rights: Public domain: historical photograph published before 1931; photographer died in 1882.

people.name: Theodore Roosevelt
people.subtitle: 26th President · An adventurous spirit
people.biography: A rancher, author, and conservationist, Roosevelt brought an energetic approach to public life.

image.attribution: Pach Brothers, Theodore Roosevelt, 1904. Library of Congress; restored by Adam Cuerden; cropped version via Wikimedia Commons.
image.rights: Public domain in the U.S. (published before 1931). Restorer grants unrestricted reuse and requests attribution.

people.name: John F. Kennedy
people.subtitle: 35th President · A new frontier
people.biography: A naval veteran who entered politics after World War II, Kennedy encouraged public service and space exploration.

image.attribution: Cecil W. Stoughton, John F. Kennedy, 1963. White House photograph; JFK Library / National Archives, via Wikimedia Commons.
image.rights: Public domain: photograph made in the course of official U.S. federal government duties.

people.name: Martha Washington
people.subtitle: First Lady · Washington administration
people.biography: Martha shaped the role of presidential spouse, supported wartime encampments, and managed an estate built on enslaved labor.

image.attribution: Unidentified artist, copy after Gilbert Stuart. Martha Washington, early–mid 19th century. National Portrait Gallery, Smithsonian Institution, NPG.70.3; via Wikimedia Commons.
image.rights: CC0 / Smithsonian Open Access; public-domain artwork.

people.name: Martha Jefferson Randolph
people.subtitle: White House hostess · Jefferson administration
people.biography: Jefferson’s daughter, known as Patsy, served as an occasional hostess. She was not his spouse.

image.attribution: Thomas Sully, Martha Jefferson Randolph. Image from Monticello via Wikimedia Commons.
image.rights: Public-domain painting and faithful reproduction; artist died in 1872.

people.name: Mary Todd Lincoln
people.subtitle: First Lady · Lincoln administration
people.biography: An educated Kentuckian, Mary and Abraham built their family life in Springfield before moving to Washington.

image.attribution: Mathew Brady, Mary Todd Lincoln, circa 1861; crop by Materialscientist via Wikimedia Commons.
image.rights: Public-domain historical photograph; Commons marks the cropped reproduction as public domain.

people.name: Edith Roosevelt
people.subtitle: First Lady · Roosevelt administration
people.biography: Edith professionalized White House social operations and helped preserve the history of the presidential home.

image.attribution: Frances Benjamin Johnston, Edith Roosevelt. Library of Congress; restored by Adam Cuerden; cropped version via Wikimedia Commons.
image.rights: Public-domain historical photograph. Restorer grants unrestricted reuse and requests attribution.

people.name: Jacqueline Kennedy
people.subtitle: First Lady · Kennedy administration
people.biography: An advocate for art and preservation, Jacqueline restored the White House and later built a career in publishing.

image.attribution: Mark Shaw, Jacqueline Kennedy, 1961; originally in Look magazine; cropped reproduction via Wikimedia Commons.
image.rights: Public domain in the U.S. due to nonrenewal of copyright as recorded by Commons; other jurisdictions may differ.

people.name: John Adams
people.subtitle: 2nd President · A lawyer abroad
people.biography: A lawyer and diplomat, John Adams argued for independence and became the second president. His presidency included both diplomacy and laws restricting dissent.

image.attribution: Gilbert Stuart, John Adams, c. 1821. National Gallery of Art, Washington; Ailsa Mellon Bruce Fund; 1979.4.1.
image.rights: Public-domain artwork; National Gallery of Art digital reproduction released under CC0. Resized to 250 pixels wide and JPEG compressed; no retouching. Display may crop and apply sepia.

people.name: Abigail Adams
people.subtitle: First Lady · Adams administration
people.biography: A reader, letter writer, and political adviser, Abigail Adams managed the family farm and challenged limits on women’s lives while also supporting restrictions on the press.

image.attribution: Gilbert Stuart, Abigail Adams, 1800/1815. National Gallery of Art, Washington; Gift of Mrs. Robert Homans; 1954.7.2.
image.rights: Public-domain artwork; National Gallery of Art digital reproduction released under CC0. Resized to 250 pixels wide and JPEG compressed; no retouching. Display may crop and apply sepia.

people.name: James Madison
people.subtitle: 4th President · Debates and contradictions
people.biography: James Madison helped shape the Constitution and Bill of Rights. He also enslaved people, a profound contradiction of the liberty he promoted.

image.attribution: Gilbert Stuart, James Madison, c. 1821. National Gallery of Art, Washington; Ailsa Mellon Bruce Fund; 1979.4.2.
image.rights: Public-domain artwork; National Gallery of Art digital reproduction released under CC0. Resized to 250 pixels wide and JPEG compressed; no retouching. Display may crop and apply sepia.

people.name: Dolley Madison
people.subtitle: First Lady · Madison administration
people.biography: Dolley Madison used hospitality to build political connections. She occasionally hosted for Jefferson before her husband’s presidency and managed a household that enslaved people.

image.attribution: Gilbert Stuart, Dolley Madison, 1804. White House Collection, 994.1737.1; faithful reproduction via Wikimedia Commons.
image.rights: Public-domain artwork (Stuart died in 1828); Commons identifies this faithful reproduction as public domain in the United States under PD-Art. Resized to 250 pixels wide and JPEG compressed; no retouching. Display may crop and apply sepia.

people.name: John Quincy Adams
people.subtitle: 6th President · A swimmer with a notebook
people.biography: A diplomat from childhood, John Quincy Adams became president and then a congressman. He loved learning and exercise; his later antislavery work also challenges us to examine his household’s reliance on enslaved labor.

image.attribution: Meade Brothers Studio, after an unidentified photographer, John Quincy Adams, c. 1860 photographic copy. National Portrait Gallery, Smithsonian Institution; gift of Mr. and Mrs. Dudley Emerson Lyons, S/NPG.85.265. CC0; detail, cropped and resized.
image.rights: CC0 — Smithsonian Open Access; exact object and media both CC0.

people.name: Louisa Catherine Adams
people.subtitle: First Lady · Music, words, and a world of travel
people.biography: Born in London and educated partly in France, Louisa was a musician, writer, and experienced traveler. She helped shape diplomatic and political life and later organized antislavery petitions.

image.attribution: G. F. Storm, after Charles Robert Leslie, Louisa Catherine Adams, 1834–1860(?). Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, LC-USZ62-14438. Cropped and resized.
image.rights: Public domain in the United States: nineteenth-century publication; LOC advisory: No known restrictions on publication.

people.name: Ulysses S. Grant
people.subtitle: 18th President · Horses, history, and hard choices
people.biography: Grant’s life stretched from horse training to Union command, the presidency, and memoir writing. He had enslaved William Jones before the war; as president, he enforced civil rights during Reconstruction.

image.attribution: Unidentified photographer, Ulysses S. Grant, c. 1876. National Portrait Gallery, Smithsonian Institution, NPG.80.183. CC0; cropped and resized.
image.rights: CC0 — Smithsonian Open Access; object and exact media both CC0.

people.name: Julia Dent Grant
people.subtitle: First Lady · A traveler with stories to tell
people.biography: Julia managed farm business, took an interest in politics, and wrote about her travels and family. Her memories also require care: she benefited from enslaved labor and described that unequal world from her own perspective.

image.attribution: Julia Dent Grant, photographed 1876, printed later; photographer unidentified. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, LC-USZ62-25791. Cropped and resized.
image.rights: Library of Congress rights advisory: No known restrictions on publication.

people.name: Calvin Coolidge
people.subtitle: 30th President · Quiet words and an electric horse
people.biography: A Vermont-born lawyer, Calvin Coolidge entered the presidency after Warren Harding’s death. Behind his reserved image were pets and unusual exercise equipment, alongside controversial choices about government spending and immigration.

image.attribution: Notman Photo Co., Calvin Coolidge as governor, 1919. Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division, LC-DIG-ppmsc-03670. Cropped and resized.
image.rights: Public domain in the United States: copyright nonrenewal recorded by LOC.

people.name: Grace Coolidge
people.subtitle: First Lady · Classrooms, baseball, and Rebecca
people.biography: Grace began as a teacher of deaf children and remained committed to education. At the White House she welcomed guests, enjoyed baseball, cared for animals, and helped preserve historic furnishings.

image.attribution: Harris & Ewing Studio, Grace Anna Goodhue Coolidge, 1931. National Portrait Gallery, Smithsonian Institution; gift of the University Women's Club, Inc. S/NPG.82.16. CC0; cropped and resized.
image.rights: CC0 — Smithsonian Open Access; object and exact media both CC0.

people.name: Jimmy Carter
people.subtitle: 39th President · A submariner with a woodshop
people.biography: A naval officer and Georgia farmer, Jimmy Carter brought interests in science and practical work to public life. After a presidency marked by diplomacy and difficult crises, he continued humanitarian work, writing, and making furniture.

image.attribution: Naval Photographic Center, James Earl “Jimmy” Carter, exposure date unidentified. National Archives at College Park, Still Pictures, 428-KN-26854, NAID 558522. U.S. federal government work; detail, cropped and resized.
image.rights: Public domain in the United States: U.S. federal agency work, Naval Photographic Center, 428-KN-26854.

people.name: Rosalynn Carter
people.subtitle: First Lady · Advocacy, accounting, and butterflies
people.biography: Rosalynn was a business partner, diplomatic envoy, and advocate for mental health and family caregivers. Her interests also included sewing, fly-fishing, and creating places where butterflies could thrive.

image.attribution: White House Staff Photographers, Official portrait of Rosalynn Carter, February 18, 1977. Jimmy Carter Library, National Archives, NAID 173749, NLC-WHSP-C-00383-08. Public domain; cropped and resized.
image.rights: Public domain in the United States: White House Staff Photographers Collection, Jimmy Carter Library / National Archives.

facts.description: Army command kept him from home for six years.

facts.description: He returned to farming after his presidency.

facts.headline: Learning many languages
facts.description: Young Jefferson studied Latin, Greek, and French.

facts.headline: College at seventeen
facts.description: He entered William and Mary in 1760.

facts.headline: An influential mentor

facts.headline: Starting in law
facts.description: His first recorded legal case dates to 1767.

facts.headline: Designing his home
facts.description: He designed the house at Monticello.

facts.headline: On the mountaintop
facts.description: Monticello construction began in 1769.

facts.headline: The Declaration’s draftsman
facts.description: He drafted the Declaration of Independence.

facts.headline: Freedom of belief
facts.description: He authored Virginia’s Statute for Religious Freedom.

facts.headline: A university founder
facts.description: He founded the University of Virginia.

facts.headline: A troubling contradiction

facts.headline: An expanding nation
facts.description: The Louisiana Purchase doubled the country’s size.

facts.headline: A daughter as hostess
facts.description: His daughter Martha sometimes served as hostess.

facts.headline: Choosing his epitaph
facts.description: His grave marker omits his presidency.

facts.headline: An extraordinary anniversary
facts.description: He died on Independence Day’s fiftieth anniversary.

facts.headline: A Kentucky beginning
facts.description: He was born near Hodgenville in 1809.

facts.headline: Teaching himself
facts.description: Lincoln was largely self-educated.

facts.headline: A lawyer’s path
facts.description: He qualified as a lawyer in 1836.

facts.headline: Statehouse experience
facts.description: He served in Illinois’s legislature from 1834–1842.

facts.headline: A Whig in Congress
facts.description: He won election to Congress in 1846.

facts.headline: Joining a new party
facts.description: He joined the Republican Party in 1856.

facts.headline: Debates without victory
facts.description: His 1858 Senate campaign ended in defeat.

facts.headline: A wartime proclamation
facts.description: He issued the Emancipation Proclamation in 1863.

facts.headline: Finding his general
facts.description: He appointed Grant overall commander in 1864.

facts.headline: A tragic ending
facts.description: He died after being shot at Ford’s Theatre.

facts.headline: Less than a year
facts.description: He received under a year of formal schooling.

facts.headline: Two left feet
facts.description: He met Mary at a Springfield dance.

facts.headline: One home of his own
facts.description: He bought his only house in Springfield.

facts.headline: Room to grow
facts.description: The Lincolns expanded their cottage to two stories.

facts.headline: Seventeen years at home
facts.description: His family lived there for seventeen years.

facts.headline: Meet Teedie
facts.description: His family called young Theodore “Teedie.”

facts.headline: A difficult childhood
facts.description: He suffered severe childhood asthma.

facts.headline: A Harvard chapter
facts.description: He began Harvard studies in 1876.

facts.headline: A western reinvention
facts.description: He worked as a Dakota Territory rancher.

facts.headline: A rancher in print
facts.description: He wrote Hunting Trips of a Ranchman.

facts.headline: A prolific author
facts.description: He wrote roughly thirty books.

facts.headline: A London wedding
facts.description: He married Edith Carow in London in 1886.

facts.headline: Before the Oval Office
facts.description: He served as New York City police commissioner.

facts.headline: The Rough Riders
facts.description: He led volunteers in the Spanish-American War.

facts.headline: A Buffalo inauguration
facts.description: He took the presidential oath in Buffalo.

facts.headline: Peace prize president
facts.description: He received the 1906 Nobel Peace Prize.

facts.headline: Protecting forests
facts.description: His presidency established 150 national forests.

facts.headline: A bird sanctuary
facts.description: He established the Pelican Island federal bird reserve.

facts.headline: A Smithsonian expedition
facts.description: He collected African specimens for the Smithsonian.

facts.headline: The River of Doubt
facts.description: He explored a Brazilian river with Kermit.

facts.headline: Meet Jack
facts.description: Family and friends called him Jack.

facts.headline: A big family
facts.description: He was one of nine Kennedy children.

facts.headline: A Boston namesake
facts.description: He was named for his maternal grandfather.

facts.headline: A young newspaper reader
facts.description: At Choate, he subscribed to the New York Times.

facts.headline: A book from a thesis
facts.description: His thesis became Why England Slept.

facts.headline: Harvard graduate
facts.description: He graduated from Harvard in 1940.

facts.headline: Commanding PT-109
facts.description: He commanded a Pacific patrol torpedo boat.

facts.headline: A message on a coconut
facts.description: He carved a rescue message into coconut shell.

facts.headline: Saving a shipmate
facts.description: He towed injured Patrick McMahon to shore.

facts.headline: Recognized for courage
facts.description: He received the Navy and Marine Corps Medal.

facts.headline: Three House terms
facts.description: He served six years in the House.

facts.headline: A Senate chapter
facts.description: He won a Senate seat in 1952.

facts.headline: A Pulitzer winner
facts.description: Profiles in Courage won the 1957 biography Pulitzer.

facts.headline: Elected at forty-three
facts.description: He was the youngest elected U.S. president.

facts.headline: Service around the world
facts.description: He created the Peace Corps.

facts.headline: Before she was Washington
facts.description: Her birth surname was Dandridge.

facts.headline: A Virginia childhood
facts.description: She was born in New Kent County.

facts.headline: A first marriage
facts.description: She married Daniel Parke Custis in 1750.

facts.headline: Four Custis children
facts.description: She had four children with Daniel Custis.

facts.headline: Widowed at twenty-six
facts.description: Daniel died in 1757.

facts.headline: Managing an estate
facts.description: She managed business interests during her widowhood.

facts.headline: Meeting George
facts.description: She met George Washington in 1758.

facts.headline: A new home
facts.description: The Washingtons settled at Mount Vernon.

facts.headline: A blended family
facts.description: They raised her surviving Custis children.

facts.headline: Winter with the army
facts.description: She visited Cambridge’s 1775–1776 winter encampment.

facts.headline: At Valley Forge
facts.description: She joined the 1777–1778 winter encampment.

facts.headline: Supplies for soldiers
facts.description: She organized clothing and supplies for troops.

facts.headline: Weekly receptions
facts.description: She hosted presidential gatherings called levees.

facts.headline: Longing for privacy
facts.description: She preferred private life at Mount Vernon.

facts.headline: Freedom, and its limits
facts.description: She freed George’s enslaved people but enslaved others.

facts.headline: Known as Patsy
facts.description: Her family called her Patsy.

facts.headline: A September birthday
facts.description: She was born September 27, 1772.

facts.headline: A daughter, not spouse
facts.description: She was Thomas Jefferson’s eldest daughter.

facts.headline: Learning beyond home
facts.description: She received a private education.

facts.headline: Traveling with her father
facts.description: She accompanied Jefferson abroad.

facts.headline: A February wedding
facts.description: She married Thomas Mann Randolph in 1790.

facts.headline: A large household
facts.description: She had twelve children.

facts.headline: Eleven reached adulthood
facts.description: Eleven of her children survived to adulthood.

facts.headline: Life at Monticello
facts.description: Her family lived at Monticello.

facts.headline: Plantation management
facts.description: She managed households and enslaved workers.

facts.headline: Two hostess seasons
facts.description: She hosted in 1802–1803 and 1805–1806.

facts.headline: A presidential-house birth
facts.description: Her son James Madison Randolph was born there.

facts.headline: Financial hardship
facts.description: Monticello was sold after Jefferson’s death.

facts.headline: Preserving her father’s papers
facts.description: She helped compile and edit Jefferson’s papers.

facts.headline: Resting at Monticello
facts.description: She died in 1836 and is buried there.

facts.headline: A Kentucky childhood
facts.description: She was born in Lexington in 1818.

facts.headline: Mary Ann
facts.description: Her birth name was Mary Ann Todd.

facts.headline: An unusual classroom
facts.description: She attended Dr. Ward’s coeducational academy.

facts.headline: More education than most
facts.description: Her schooling exceeded many contemporary women’s opportunities.

facts.headline: A family’s objections
facts.description: Some relatives disapproved of her marrying Lincoln.

facts.headline: A November wedding
facts.description: She married Abraham on November 4, 1842.

facts.headline: A Springfield farewell
facts.description: She died in Springfield in 1882.

facts.headline: Very different homes
facts.description: She grew up in a fourteen-room house.

facts.headline: Meeting on the dance floor
facts.description: She met Abraham at a dance.

facts.headline: A broken courtship
facts.description: Their courtship broke off in January 1841.

facts.headline: A secret reunion
facts.description: They resumed dating secretly through mutual friends.

facts.headline: A sister’s wedding venue
facts.description: They married at Elizabeth’s house.

facts.headline: A one-room beginning
facts.description: Their first married home was one rented room.

facts.headline: Welcoming Robert
facts.description: Their first child was born in that room.

facts.headline: Moving in May
facts.description: They moved into their house in May 1844.

facts.headline: A Manhattan beginning
facts.description: Edith Carow was born in Manhattan in 1861.

facts.headline: Childhood connections
facts.description: She was friends with Theodore’s sister Corinne.

facts.headline: Learning at home
facts.description: Tutors provided most of her early education.

facts.headline: A private-school chapter
facts.description: She later attended Miss Comstock’s school.

facts.headline: Teenage letters
facts.description: She and Theodore exchanged letters as teenagers.

facts.headline: A chance reunion
facts.description: They reconnected at Theodore’s sister Anna’s home.

facts.headline: A December wedding
facts.description: They married December 2, 1886.

facts.headline: A Long Island home
facts.description: They settled at Sagamore Hill.

facts.headline: A blended household
facts.description: She raised Alice and five more children.

facts.headline: Running the estate
facts.description: She managed Sagamore Hill’s finances and personnel.

facts.headline: A social secretary
facts.description: She hired Isabella Hagner, the first White House social secretary.

facts.headline: Gardens for gatherings
facts.description: She added two colonial gardens.

facts.headline: A historic renovation
facts.description: She helped oversee the 1902 White House renovation.

facts.headline: Presidential china on display
facts.description: She commissioned cabinets for presidential china.

facts.headline: Remembering the first ladies
facts.description: She proposed displaying first ladies’ portraits downstairs.

facts.headline: A Southampton beginning
facts.description: She was born in Southampton in 1929.

facts.headline: A champion rider
facts.description: She won national riding championships by eleven.

facts.headline: A year in Paris
facts.description: She studied abroad during college.

facts.headline: Changing colleges
facts.description: She transferred from Vassar to George Washington University.

facts.headline: A Newport wedding
facts.description: She married Kennedy in Newport in 1953.

facts.headline: The campaign columnist
facts.description: She wrote the weekly column Campaign Wife.

facts.headline: First lady at thirty-one
facts.description: She was thirty-one at Kennedy’s inauguration.

facts.headline: A White House classroom
facts.description: She created a kindergarten on the sun porch.

facts.headline: A curator for history
facts.description: She established the White House curator’s position.

facts.headline: A televised tour
facts.description: Eighty million Americans watched her White House tour.

facts.headline: An honorary Emmy
facts.description: Her televised tour earned an honorary Emmy.

facts.headline: Languages across borders
facts.description: She spoke French, Spanish, and Italian.

facts.headline: Choosing the library architect
facts.description: She selected I.M. Pei for Kennedy’s library.

facts.headline: A publishing career
facts.description: She worked as an editor at Viking and Doubleday.

facts.headline: Saving a landmark
facts.description: She campaigned to preserve Grand Central Station.

facts.headline: From classroom to courtroom
facts.description: After graduating from Harvard in 1755, John Adams taught school in Worcester before studying law.

facts.headline: A difficult defense
facts.description: John Adams defended British soldiers accused after the Boston Massacre, despite his opposition to British policies.

facts.headline: Choosing a commander
facts.description: John Adams proposed George Washington to lead the Continental Army.

facts.headline: A Dutch diplomatic success
facts.description: In 1782, John Adams helped secure Dutch recognition of American independence and a loan for the United States.

facts.headline: Signing for peace
facts.description: John Adams helped negotiate and signed the 1783 Treaty of Paris recognizing American independence.

facts.headline: First in a new office
facts.description: John Adams served as the first United States vice president before becoming the second president.

facts.headline: Moving into the new capital
facts.description: John and Abigail Adams became the first occupants of the presidential mansion in Washington in November 1800.

facts.headline: Limits on dissent
facts.description: John Adams signed the 1798 Alien and Sedition Acts. These laws restricted immigrants and punished certain writings against the government.

facts.headline: A friendship renewed by letters
facts.description: After a political falling-out, John Adams and Thomas Jefferson renewed their correspondence in 1812.

facts.headline: A farmer in retirement
facts.description: At Peacefield in Quincy, John Adams enjoyed farming as well as reading and writing in his study.

facts.headline: Learning from books
facts.description: Abigail Adams educated herself with books from her father’s library when formal educational opportunities for girls were limited.

facts.headline: An education in helping
facts.description: As a girl, Abigail Adams accompanied her mother on visits bringing supplies to families in need.

facts.headline: A wedding at home
facts.description: Abigail Smith married John Adams in 1764, with her father conducting the wedding.

facts.headline: The farm kept going
facts.description: While John Adams served in Congress, Abigail Adams managed the farm and taught their children.

facts.headline: News across the distance
facts.description: Abigail Adams’s letters kept John Adams informed about events around Boston during the Revolution.

facts.headline: Remembering women in the laws
facts.description: In her March 1776 letter, Abigail Adams asked John Adams to “Remember the Ladies” when making new laws.

facts.headline: Challenging a contradiction
facts.description: Abigail Adams criticized Americans who fought for their own freedom while denying freedom to enslaved Black people.

facts.headline: Across the Atlantic
facts.description: Abigail Adams sailed to Europe in 1784, joining John Adams and meeting people in Paris and London.

facts.headline: Advice the president valued
facts.description: John Adams sought Abigail Adams’s advice during his presidency, including when political divisions made governing difficult.

facts.headline: A troubling position on the press
facts.description: Abigail Adams supported the Alien and Sedition Acts, believing restrictions on the opposition press would protect her husband’s government.

facts.headline: A college with a different name
facts.description: James Madison graduated in 1771 from the College of New Jersey, now Princeton University.

facts.headline: Ideas for a new government
facts.description: James Madison’s ideas helped form the Virginia Plan, introduced at the 1787 Constitutional Convention by Edmund Randolph.

facts.headline: Notes from a great debate
facts.description: James Madison recorded debates at the Constitutional Convention. His notes help historians study how the Constitution took shape.

facts.headline: A team of essay writers
facts.description: James Madison joined Alexander Hamilton and John Jay in writing The Federalist essays to support the Constitution.

facts.headline: A change of mind on rights
facts.description: James Madison initially argued a bill of rights was unnecessary, then helped guide amendments through the first Congress.

facts.headline: A diplomatic partnership
facts.description: Before becoming president, James Madison served as secretary of state under Thomas Jefferson.

facts.headline: War during his presidency
facts.description: The United States declared war on Great Britain in 1812 during James Madison’s presidency. British troops burned the White House in 1814.

facts.headline: Liberty denied at home
facts.description: James Madison enslaved people at Montpelier and brought enslaved workers to the White House, denying them the freedom he promoted in politics.

facts.headline: A library proposal before its time
facts.description: In 1783, James Madison’s congressional committee proposed about 1,300 books for Congress. The proposal was turned down over the cost.

facts.headline: A wedding anniversary shared
facts.description: James Madison married Dolley in 1794 on September 15, the same calendar date as his parents’ wedding.

facts.headline: A North Carolina beginning
facts.description: Dolley Madison was born in North Carolina in 1768, while her parents were helping establish a Quaker community.

facts.headline: A family changed by illness
facts.description: Before marrying James Madison, Dolley lost her first husband, John Todd, and their youngest son to Philadelphia’s 1793 yellow fever epidemic.

facts.headline: An introduction by Aaron Burr
facts.description: Aaron Burr introduced Dolley to James Madison in 1794. The couple married that September.

facts.headline: Hosting for another administration
facts.description: Dolley Madison occasionally hosted events for the widowed Thomas Jefferson when his daughters were unavailable. She was James Madison’s spouse.

facts.headline: Rooms with an architect
facts.description: Dolley Madison worked with architect Benjamin Henry Latrobe on White House interiors, including American-made furnishings and artwork.

facts.headline: Wednesday conversations
facts.description: Dolley Madison’s weekly White House receptions brought political opponents together for conversation and cooperation.

facts.headline: Politics through a social network
facts.description: Dolley Madison exchanged letters and visits to gather political news and help friends and family seek jobs.

facts.headline: Saving a portrait took many hands
facts.description: Before fleeing the White House in 1814, Dolley Madison ordered the Washington portrait saved. Paul Jennings’s memoir credits staff with removing it.

facts.headline: Enslavement at Montpelier
facts.description: Dolley Madison managed enslaved workers at Montpelier. Later, financial troubles led her to sell enslaved people, treating human beings as property.

facts.headline: A return to Washington
facts.description: After James Madison died, Dolley returned to Washington in 1837 and lived on Lafayette Square.

facts.headline: A child on a diplomatic voyage
facts.description: At ten, John Quincy crossed the Atlantic with his father on a diplomatic mission to France. His education stretched far beyond a classroom.

facts.headline: A teenage interpreter
facts.description: In 1781, fourteen-year-old John Quincy went to Russia with diplomat Francis Dana. He worked as a secretary and French interpreter.

facts.headline: A diary across decades
facts.description: John Quincy kept a diary for decades, recording public events alongside his own daily life. Those pages help historians look beyond his serious portraits.

facts.headline: An early-morning swimmer
facts.description: As president, John Quincy sometimes rose at five in the morning to swim in the Potomac River. Exercise was part of his daily routine.

facts.headline: An eye on the stars
facts.description: President Adams wanted the nation to build an astronomical observatory. Studying the sky belonged in his plans for the country’s future.

facts.headline: Back to Congress
facts.description: Leaving the presidency did not end Adams’s public career. He won a seat in the House of Representatives and returned to Washington as a lawmaker.

facts.headline: A complicated antislavery record
facts.description: Adams later fought slavery in Congress, but enslaved people also worked in his White House household. They had been brought there by relatives of Louisa.

facts.headline: The Amistad case
facts.description: In 1841, long after his presidency, Adams argued for the African captives from the Amistad before the Supreme Court. He helped win their freedom.

facts.headline: A canal’s first day
facts.description: On July 4, 1828, President Adams helped begin construction of the Chesapeake and Ohio Canal. Canals were part of his vision for connecting the country.

facts.headline: The swimmer and the reporter
facts.description: According to a popular story, reporter Anne Royall sat on Adams’s clothes until he agreed to an interview after swimming. Scholars consider this tale apocryphal: a story, not an established event.

facts.headline: A London beginning
facts.description: Louisa was born in London in 1775. She became the first U.S. first lady born outside the United States.

facts.headline: A childhood in French
facts.description: During the American Revolution, Louisa’s family moved to France. She learned French at school, a language that would help her throughout a traveling life.

facts.headline: Music for her guests
facts.description: Louisa played both harp and piano. At the White House, she sometimes performed for visitors herself.

facts.headline: Silkworms at the White House
facts.description: Louisa raised silkworms on the White House grounds and collected their silk for her own projects. These tiny creatures were part of her busy household.

facts.headline: Her own words
facts.description: Louisa wrote letters, stories, poems, and plays. Writing gave her a voice beyond the public role of a president’s wife.

facts.headline: Six weeks on the road
facts.description: After arranging the family’s affairs in Russia, Louisa traveled to Paris with her young son Charles. Their difficult winter journey took six weeks.

facts.headline: Work at the State Department
facts.description: When John Quincy became secretary of state in 1817, Louisa helped him as a secretary. Together they worked long hours to organize the department.

facts.headline: Politics over dinner
facts.description: Before the 1824 election, Louisa hosted Tuesday-evening dinners and dancing for political guests. She used those gatherings to build support for John Quincy.

facts.headline: Petitions needed a reader
facts.description: Louisa sorted, listed, and summarized antislavery petitions sent to her husband in Congress. Her work helped the campaign against rules that silenced them.

facts.headline: A family wedding indoors
facts.description: In 1828, Louisa hosted the White House wedding of her son John Adams II and her niece Mary Catherine Hellen.

facts.headline: A name that stuck
facts.description: Grant was born Hiram Ulysses Grant. A mistaken West Point roster called him Ulysses S. Grant, and that became the name he used.

facts.headline: The neighborhood horse expert
facts.description: Even as a boy in Ohio, Grant trained horses for neighbors. His skill with animals appeared long before his fame as a general.

facts.headline: Letters about horse care
facts.description: In an 1866 letter, Grant discussed treatment for horses’ feet and reported trying it on four of his own horses. He paid close attention to their health.

facts.headline: A different classroom dream
facts.description: As a young man, Grant considered becoming a mathematics teacher. His future did not always point toward an army uniform.

facts.headline: Leading the Union armies
facts.description: In March 1864, Grant became commanding general of all Union armies. In April 1865, he accepted Robert E. Lee’s surrender of the Army of Northern Virginia.

facts.headline: William Jones’s freedom
facts.description: Grant once enslaved a man named William Jones. On March 29, 1859, he signed a legal document freeing Jones instead of selling him.

facts.headline: Enforcing civil rights
facts.description: As president during Reconstruction, Grant used federal troops and prosecutions against Ku Klux Klan violence. These efforts protected Black communities, though they did not end racist violence.

facts.headline: A park protected by law
facts.description: In 1872, President Grant signed the law establishing Yellowstone National Park. A remarkable landscape gained federal protection.

facts.headline: A writer with a famous publisher
facts.description: After losing his fortune, Grant wrote his memoirs to help support his family. Mark Twain helped arrange their publication, and the books became bestsellers.

facts.headline: A scandal in his administration
facts.description: The Whiskey Ring cheated the government out of taxes during Grant’s presidency. Officials were involved; Grant’s private secretary was accused but acquitted.

facts.headline: An outdoors childhood
facts.description: Growing up at White Haven in Missouri, Julia fished, rode horses, and played in the woods. She liked a world bigger than the parlor.

facts.headline: An engagement that waited
facts.description: Julia and Ulysses became engaged in 1844, but his service in the Mexican-American War delayed their wedding until 1848.

facts.headline: Chickens, butter, and unequal work
facts.description: Julia raised chickens and churned butter at White Haven. Much of the household cooking was done by enslaved people, whose labor supported the family.

facts.headline: Managing the farm’s business
facts.description: During the Civil War, Julia managed White Haven’s finances. She collected rent, leased land, and handled property paperwork while her husband was away.

facts.headline: More than a hostess
facts.description: As first lady, Julia attended Senate hearings, read presidential mail, and met officials and diplomats. She took an active interest in government.

facts.headline: Nellie’s East Room wedding
facts.description: Julia’s daughter Nellie married in the White House East Room in 1874. Family celebrations were part of Julia’s life as first lady.

facts.headline: Around the world afterward
facts.description: After the presidency ended in 1877, Julia and Ulysses took a world tour lasting about two and a half years. She later devoted a large part of her memoirs to it.

facts.headline: A book that waited decades
facts.description: Julia wrote the first memoir by a U.S. first lady, but it was not published during her lifetime. Readers finally received the full book in 1975.

facts.headline: Jule chose freedom
facts.description: Jule, enslaved by Julia’s father, worked as Julia’s nurse and maid during the Civil War. In early 1864, she escaped in Louisville and began a life beyond the Grants’ control.

facts.headline: A Fourth of July birthday
facts.description: Calvin Coolidge was born in Vermont on July 4, 1872. His birthday fell on the same day Americans celebrate Independence Day.

facts.headline: An oath by lamplight
facts.description: After President Harding died in 1923, Coolidge took the presidential oath at his father’s home in Vermont. His father administered it by the light of a kerosene lamp.

facts.headline: A horse that stayed indoors
facts.description: Coolidge exercised on an electric horse in the White House. The machine could imitate a trot or a gallop without going anywhere.

facts.headline: Two traveling collies
facts.description: The Coolidge family took their collies Rob Roy and Prudence Prim on their summer trip to South Dakota. Presidential travel could include paws.

facts.headline: Small government, big arguments
facts.description: Coolidge favored lower taxes and limited federal spending. He twice vetoed farm-relief bills, even as many farmers struggled.

facts.headline: A law that shut people out
facts.description: Coolidge signed the Immigration Act of 1924. Its quotas favored some national origins over others, and its racial restrictions barred many Asian immigrants.

facts.headline: Quiet, but often photographed
facts.description: Although people nicknamed him Silent Cal, Coolidge frequently posed for photographs. He understood that public images mattered.

facts.headline: The famous two-word story
facts.description: Legend has it that a dinner guest bet she could make Coolidge say more than two words. He supposedly answered, “You lose.” A later review calls this famous tale a likely invention.

facts.headline: A teacher before the White House
facts.description: Before becoming first lady, Grace trained and taught at the Clarke School for the Deaf in Massachusetts. Education remained important throughout her life.

facts.headline: A baseball-loving first lady
facts.description: Grace attended baseball games and welcomed celebrities to the White House. Sports and popular culture were part of her public life.

facts.headline: A raccoon at the Egg Roll
facts.description: Grace brought the family’s raccoon, Rebecca, to the 1927 White House Easter Egg Roll. Children met a very unusual presidential pet.

facts.headline: Rebecca’s bathtub games
facts.description: Grace later remembered Rebecca playing in a partly filled bathtub with a bar of soap. Her recollection gives a lively glimpse of the family’s pet.

facts.headline: Five canaries on vacation
facts.description: Grace’s five canaries joined the Coolidges’ planned pet travelers for their South Dakota vacation. The family’s animals were quite a traveling group.

facts.headline: Bringing history back indoors
facts.description: Grace worked to bring historic furnishings back to the White House. A 1925 congressional resolution allowed gifts of art and furniture to help the effort.

facts.headline: Service beyond her title
facts.description: After leaving the White House, Grace continued supporting deaf education. She served on the Clarke School’s board and later became its president.

facts.headline: A family’s painful loss
facts.description: Grace and Calvin’s younger son, Calvin Jr., died in 1924 after an infected tennis blister. Their White House years included deep grief as well as celebrations.

facts.headline: Science beneath the waves
facts.description: Before politics, Carter served as a Navy submariner. He studied reactor technology and nuclear physics while preparing for work in the nuclear submarine program.

facts.headline: Back to the family business
facts.description: After leaving the Navy in 1953, Jimmy returned to Georgia. He and Rosalynn ran a farm-supply and seed business alongside the Carter farms.

facts.headline: A workshop break
facts.description: After his presidency, Carter took breaks from writing his memoirs by making furniture. He recalled building more than thirty pieces while working on the book.

facts.headline: A book with Amy’s pictures
facts.description: Carter wrote a children’s book called The Little Baby Snoogle-Fleejer. His daughter Amy illustrated it.

facts.headline: Talks at Camp David
facts.description: In 1978, President Carter helped leaders of Egypt and Israel reach the Camp David Accords. Those talks helped prepare the way for a peace treaty.

facts.headline: Energy gets a department
facts.description: During Carter’s presidency, the government created the Department of Energy. Finding ways to meet the country’s energy needs became a major challenge.

facts.headline: Hostages and a difficult final year
facts.description: During Carter’s last year in office, 52 Americans remained hostage in Iran. They were released on the day he left the presidency in January 1981.

facts.headline: A Nobel after the presidency
facts.description: Carter received the Nobel Peace Prize in 2002, more than twenty years after leaving office. The award recognized decades of work for peace and human rights.

facts.headline: Building alongside volunteers
facts.description: Long after the White House, Jimmy and Rosalynn volunteered with Habitat for Humanity. They helped people renovate and build homes.

facts.headline: The numbers behind the peanuts
facts.description: Back in Georgia, Rosalynn handled accounting for the family’s peanut farm and warehouse. Her partnership with Jimmy included balancing the books.

facts.headline: Mental health belonged in public life
facts.description: As honorary chair of the President’s Commission on Mental Health, Rosalynn pressed for better care. She helped make mental health a national policy concern.

facts.headline: Supporting the people who care
facts.description: An institute established in Rosalynn’s honor in 1987 supported family caregivers. She served as president of its board, helping draw attention to people caring for loved ones.

facts.headline: An envoy with her own mission
facts.description: In 1977, Rosalynn led a U.S. delegation to seven Latin American and Caribbean countries. She traveled as a diplomatic envoy, not simply as a guest.

facts.headline: The same gown, another celebration
facts.description: Rosalynn wore a gown from Jimmy’s Georgia governor inauguration again at the presidential inaugural ball. A special dress could have more than one big night.

facts.headline: Clothes made at home
facts.description: Rosalynn sewed clothes for her daughter Amy. She stopped when the demands of life in the Georgia Governor’s Mansion left too little time.

facts.headline: A quiet stream
facts.description: Rosalynn enjoyed fly-fishing, birdwatching, and gardening. Outdoor interests were part of her life alongside public service.

facts.headline: Gardens for butterflies
facts.description: Rosalynn championed monarch butterflies and inspired the Rosalynn Carter Butterfly Trail. Its gardens provide habitat for butterflies and other pollinators.

facts.headline: A new center after Washington
facts.description: In 1982, after leaving the White House, Rosalynn and Jimmy founded The Carter Center. Its work connected peace, human rights, and better health.

facts.headline: First in her class
facts.description: Rosalynn graduated from Plains High School as valedictorian in 1944. The future first lady had been the student chosen to lead her graduating class academically.
